question_text: A company's FM costs are rising rapidly because prompts include unnecessary context. Which techniques reduce token usage without significantly degrading output quality? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Context pruning — removing irrelevant prior conversation turns from the context window
Prompt compression — summarising verbose context into a concise form before FM invocation
Increasing the maxTokens parameter to allow more complete responses
Using a larger FM to process tokens more efficiently
Adding more detailed instructions to every prompt

explanation: Skill 4.1.1 describes context pruning and prompt compression as token efficiency techniques. Context pruning removes stale or irrelevant turns (e.g., greetings, resolved sub-tasks). Prompt compression uses techniques like summarisation to shorten verbose inputs. Both reduce billable input tokens. Increasing maxTokens raises the cost ceiling per call. Larger FMs cost more per token. Adding more instructions increases input token count.
source_topic: Token efficiency, prompt compression, context pruning

question_text: A customer support GenAI application receives many semantically identical questions phrased differently (e.g., 'How do I reset my password?' vs 'I forgot my password, how do I change it?'). Calling the FM for each is wasteful. What caching approach addresses this?

options.text: Exact string match caching — only cache when the query is byte-for-byte identical
Semantic caching — embed incoming queries, search a cache by vector similarity, and return a cached response if similarity exceeds a threshold
Cache all responses for 1 hour regardless of query content
Disable caching and call the FM for every query

explanation: Skill 4.1.4 explicitly describes semantic caching using vector similarity. Embedding the query and comparing against cached query embeddings allows cache hits for semantically equivalent but lexically different questions. Exact string matching misses paraphrase variants. Time-based blanket caching returns stale responses for time-sensitive questions. No caching maximises FM cost.
source_topic: Semantic caching, vector similarity, cost optimisation

question_text: A company processes millions of queries daily. 80% are simple FAQ lookups; 20% require complex reasoning. How should FM selection be optimised for cost?

options.text: Use the most expensive large FM for all queries to ensure maximum quality
Use a tiered approach: route simple queries to a small cheap FM; escalate complex queries to a large capable FM based on query complexity classification
Use a single medium-cost FM for all queries as a compromise
Disable the FM for the 80% of simple queries and return static responses only

explanation: Skill 4.1.2 describes tiered FM usage based on query complexity and cost-capability tradeoff evaluation. A routing classifier (simple rule-based or a tiny FM) identifies query type; simple FAQs use a cheap model (e.g., Titan Lite), complex reasoning uses a powerful model (e.g., Claude 3 Opus). A single medium model over-spends on 80% of queries. Static responses for simple queries lose GenAI quality benefits.

question_text: A company processes 100,000 document summaries nightly using Bedrock. On-demand API calls result in throttling and high per-token costs. Which approach maximises resource utilisation and reduces cost for this predictable batch workload?

options.text: Spread requests across 24 hours to avoid throttling
Use Amazon Bedrock Batch Inference with appropriately sized Provisioned Throughput — batch all 100K documents into a single job and process overnight at discounted batch pricing
Use a single Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout to process all documents
Move all processing to an EC2 instance with a self-hosted model

explanation: Skill 4.1.3 describes batching strategies and provisioned throughput optimisation for predictable GenAI workloads. Bedrock Batch Inference lets you submit large document sets as a batch job at significantly lower per-token pricing compared to on-demand. Provisioned Throughput provides reserved capacity for sustained throughput. Spreading over 24 hours uses on-demand pricing throughout. A single Lambda can run only 15 minutes. Self-hosted EC2 adds operational overhead.
source_topic: Bedrock Batch Inference, Provisioned Throughput, batching

question_text: An application includes a very long system prompt (10,000 tokens) in every API call because the instructions rarely change. This makes every call expensive. Which Bedrock feature reduces repeated cost for static prompt prefixes?

options.text: Reduce the system prompt to 100 tokens and lose the detailed instructions
Amazon Bedrock prompt caching — cache the static system prompt so it is only processed once and reused across calls
Store the system prompt in DynamoDB and retrieve it on each call
Use a separate FM call to summarise the system prompt before each invocation

explanation: Skill 4.1.4 explicitly cites prompt caching. Bedrock prompt caching allows a static prefix (e.g., a long system prompt) to be processed once and reused across subsequent calls, dramatically reducing input token costs for applications with large static prompts. Truncating instructions degrades quality. Retrieving from DynamoDB still submits the full prompt to the FM every time. A separate summarisation call adds cost and degrades instruction fidelity.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, cost optimisation

question_text: An e-commerce platform uses Bedrock in us-east-1 to generate product descriptions. During flash sales, requests spike and hit 'ThrottlingException: Too many requests.' The solution must increase throughput using the exact same FM at minimum extra cost, with no additional operational code.

options.text: Purchase Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for reserved capacity
Use Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference — switch to an Inference Profile ARN so AWS automatically routes overflow to other regions' quotas
Write a Lambda that retries on a secondary region on ThrottlingException
Use Bedrock Prompt Router to distribute requests across multiple FM families

explanation: Skill 4.1.3 and 1.2.3 describe Cross-Region Inference for throughput optimisation. Replacing the model ID with a Cross-Region Inference Profile ARN delegates routing to AWS: it pools capacity across multiple regions within a geographic area, effectively multiplying available quota with zero custom code. Provisioned Throughput (A) fixes throttling but commits to 24/7 reserved capacity charges — very expensive for spiky flash-sale traffic. A Lambda retry (C) is exactly the manual implementation that Cross-Region Inference replaces. Prompt Router (D) routes between FM families — it uses different models and violates the 'same FM' requirement.
source_topic: Bedrock Cross-Region Inference, throttling, cost optimisation

question_text: A government agency operates under regulations that require all AI inference and training data to remain physically within a specific country that has no AWS Region. They need to use AWS-managed GenAI services without data leaving their premises. Which infrastructure option addresses this?

options.text: AWS Outposts — extends AWS infrastructure and services to on-premises locations, keeping data and compute physically within the required jurisdiction
AWS Local Zones — extend AWS closer to end users but still reside outside the customer's premises
Amazon CloudFront edge locations — cache content globally but do not support ML inference on-premises
Use a public AWS Region and rely on encryption alone

explanation: AWS Outposts brings AWS compute, storage, and services physically to the customer's on-premises facility, keeping all data within the premises and under the customer's physical control. This satisfies strict data-residency or data-sovereignty laws. Local Zones reduce latency but are AWS-operated infrastructure outside the customer's building. CloudFront is a CDN, not compute for ML. Encryption alone does not address data-residency requirements when the hardware is in a foreign region.
source_topic: AWS Outposts, data residency, on-premises GenAI

question_text: A company spends $5,000/month on Amazon Bedrock inference. Analysis shows that 40% of the cost comes from long conversation histories being re-sent with every message. What is the MOST direct cost optimisation?

options.text: Switch to a more expensive but faster model
Prune or summarise old conversation history in DynamoDB before adding to the prompt — reduce input tokens per request
Enable Bedrock Cross-Region Inference to distribute cost
Add more Lambda concurrency to process requests faster

explanation: Total cost = (input tokens + output tokens) × price per token. Pruning or summarising old conversation history before including it in each prompt directly reduces input tokens per request — the largest cost driver identified. Switching to a more expensive model increases cost. Cross-Region Inference spreads load but doesn't reduce token count. More Lambda concurrency doesn't reduce per-request token usage.
source_topic: Context window pruning to reduce input token costs

question_text: An e-commerce GenAI assistant frequently receives questions like 'How do I return a product?', 'What is your return policy?', and 'How can I send back an item?' — semantically equivalent but textually different. The team wants to cache and reuse responses for these similar queries. What caching technique handles paraphrases?

options.text: Exact-match hash caching in ElastiCache (Redis)
CloudFront edge caching of the GET response
Semantic caching: embed the incoming query, search a vector store (MemoryDB/OpenSearch) for similar cached queries, return cached response if similarity exceeds threshold
DynamoDB TTL-based response cache

explanation: Semantic caching embeds each incoming query and searches a vector store for previously cached queries with high embedding similarity. If similarity exceeds the threshold, the cached response is returned — handling paraphrases, synonyms, and rewordings. Exact-match hash caching (A) only matches identical strings. CloudFront caches URL-based GET requests, not semantic content. DynamoDB TTL caching requires exact key matches.
source_topic: Semantic caching with MemoryDB/OpenSearch for paraphrase handling

question_text: A GenAI platform serves multiple internal departments and needs to track Bedrock inference costs by department for monthly chargeback. Department IDs must appear in cost allocation reports. What is the MOST operationally simple approach?

options.text: Create a separate AWS account per department and use AWS Organizations for cost aggregation
Tag each Lambda function with department cost allocation tags and use AWS Cost Explorer to filter by tag
Log department_id and token counts to CloudWatch; use a Lambda to aggregate and report monthly costs
Track invocation counts manually in a spreadsheet

explanation: Cost allocation tags on AWS resources (Lambda functions, API Gateway stages) flow through to Cost Explorer, enabling filtering and grouping by department for chargeback reports. This is the most operationally simple approach — no custom aggregation code needed. Separate accounts per department adds significant overhead. Custom Lambda aggregation requires code maintenance. Manual spreadsheets don't scale.
source_topic: Cost allocation tags + Cost Explorer for department chargeback

topic: Bedrock Batch Inference for large-scale processing
question_text: A team needs to generate summaries for 2 million archived support tickets. Processing them in real time via synchronous InvokeModel calls is too expensive (overhead per call) and takes days. What is the MOST cost-efficient approach?

options.text: Use Lambda with 1000 concurrent functions, each calling InvokeModel
Use Bedrock Batch Inference (StartBatchInferenceJob) to process all tickets from S3 asynchronously at bulk pricing
Purchase Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for high-volume processing
Run inference on a SageMaker real-time endpoint

explanation: Bedrock Batch Inference is purpose-built for large-scale async processing — submit all 2M tickets to S3 in JSONL format, trigger StartBatchInferenceJob, and results are written back to S3. Batch pricing is lower than per-request pricing. Lambda concurrency (A) still incurs per-request pricing and concurrency overhead. Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for steady traffic, not batch processing. SageMaker endpoints require custom container management.
source_topic: Bedrock Batch Inference for cost-efficient large-scale processing

question_text: A company spends $8,000/month on Claude Sonnet for all requests. Analysis shows 60% of requests are simple FAQ lookups that a smaller model handles equally well. Which architectural change reduces costs MOST significantly while maintaining quality?

options.text: Switch all traffic to Claude Haiku regardless of complexity
Implement model cascading: route to Claude Haiku first; only escalate to Claude Sonnet if Haiku's confidence is below threshold
Reduce max_tokens by 50% for all requests
Enable prompt caching for all Claude Sonnet calls

explanation: Model cascading routes 60% of simple requests to the cheaper Haiku and only uses expensive Sonnet for the complex 40%. This preserves quality for hard cases while dramatically reducing average cost per request. Switching everything to Haiku (A) risks quality degradation on complex requests. Reducing max_tokens across the board may truncate valid responses. Prompt caching helps for repeated system prompts but doesn't address the per-request model selection problem.
source_topic: Model cascading to route simple requests to cheaper models

question_text: A company processes three request types: (1) simple yes/no classification, (2) 500-word document summarisation, (3) complex multi-document legal analysis. They want to minimise total monthly cost while maintaining acceptable quality for each type. What is the BEST model assignment?

options.text: All three: Claude Sonnet for consistency
(1) Amazon Titan Text Lite, (2) Claude Haiku, (3) Claude Sonnet — tiered by complexity and cost
All three: Amazon Titan Text Lite for minimum cost
(1) Claude Sonnet, (2) Claude Haiku, (3) Titan Text Lite

explanation: The correct tiered assignment matches model capability to task complexity: (1) Yes/no classification is a simple factual task → Titan Text Lite (lowest cost). (2) Document summarisation requires moderate reasoning → Claude Haiku (balanced cost/capability). (3) Complex multi-document legal analysis demands advanced reasoning → Claude Sonnet. Using Claude Sonnet for everything (A) maximises cost. Using Titan Lite for everything (C) degrades quality on tasks 2 and 3. Option D reverses the cost-complexity mapping.
source_topic: Tiered FM selection: matching model capability to task complexity

question_text: A developer notices that their Bedrock API calls include very long system prompts (2,000 tokens) that are identical across all requests. These tokens are charged on every call. What optimisation reduces this repetitive cost?

options.text: Remove the system prompt entirely
Implement Bedrock prompt caching — cache the system prompt prefix to avoid re-charging those tokens on each call
Store the system prompt in DynamoDB and append it dynamically
Compress the system prompt using gzip before sending

explanation: Bedrock prompt caching allows a common prefix (like a long system prompt) to be cached so that repeated calls with the same prefix don't re-charge those input tokens. This can reduce input token costs by up to 90% for applications with long, static system prompts. Removing the system prompt loses important FM behaviour guidance. DynamoDB doesn't help — tokens are still charged when the prompt is sent. gzip is not a valid Bedrock API option.
source_topic: Bedrock prompt caching for repeated system prompt cost reduction

question_text: A SageMaker real-time inference endpoint needs to scale out automatically when the queue of pending inference requests grows (indicating processing backlog). Which auto-scaling metric is MOST appropriate for this use case?

options.text: CPUUtilization — scale when CPU exceeds 70%
InvocationCount — scale when total invocations exceed a threshold
ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible on the input SQS queue — scale when queue depth grows
ModelLatency — scale when response time exceeds 2 seconds

explanation: When using SQS as a buffer in front of SageMaker inference (a common async pattern), the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric reflects the actual backlog. Scaling the endpoint based on queue depth ensures capacity keeps pace with incoming work regardless of CPU or latency patterns. CPUUtilization indicates compute pressure but lags behind the actual queue. InvocationCount measures throughput, not backlog. ModelLatency reacts after users are already affected.
source_topic: SQS queue depth for SageMaker auto-scaling in async patterns

question_text: A company uses Bedrock on-demand pricing and consistently hits ThrottlingException errors during business hours (8 AM–6 PM weekdays), while overnight usage is near zero. They want to eliminate throttling during business hours without paying for capacity overnight. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?

options.text: Purchase 24/7 Provisioned Throughput for the required business-hours capacity
Implement exponential backoff — the throttling will self-resolve
Purchase Provisioned Throughput scheduled for business hours only, combined with on-demand for overflow or off-hours
Switch to a different, less popular model to avoid throttling queues

explanation: Bedrock Provisioned Throughput can be purchased for specific time windows (business hours), reducing the cost vs. 24/7 commitment. Combining with on-demand for overnight/overflow handles the rare cases without wasted provisioned capacity. 24/7 provisioning is wasteful given zero overnight usage. Exponential backoff helps transient throttling but doesn't solve sustained capacity shortfall. Switching models may degrade quality.
source_topic: Scheduled Provisioned Throughput for business-hours peak capacity

question_text: A developer's Bedrock application often receives verbose responses with unnecessary padding ('Certainly! I would be happy to help you with that. Here is the information you requested:...'). What is the SIMPLEST way to reduce output token count and cost?

options.text: Post-process all responses to remove preamble text with regex
Set a lower max_tokens value and instruct the model in the system prompt: 'Be concise. Answer directly without preamble.'
Fine-tune the model to produce shorter responses
Switch to a different model that is naturally more concise

explanation: The simplest fix is a system prompt instruction for conciseness combined with a lower max_tokens limit to cap response length. System prompts like 'Answer directly without preamble' significantly reduce verbose padding. max_tokens prevents runaway verbose responses. Regex post-processing (A) is brittle and doesn't reduce charged tokens (you pay for generated tokens even if you discard them). Fine-tuning (C) is expensive for this minor issue.
source_topic: System prompt + max_tokens for output token cost reduction

question_text: A team has purchased Bedrock Provisioned Throughput and is monitoring ModelInvocationUtilization. The metric shows 85% utilisation consistently. What does this indicate and what should they do?

options.text: 85% is too high — add more model units immediately
85% is in the optimal range (70-90%) for cost-efficiency — no action needed
85% means the model is degraded — switch to on-demand
85% utilisation triggers automatic scaling of provisioned units

explanation: For Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, the target utilisation for cost-efficiency is 70-90%. At 85%, the team is getting good value from their provisioned capacity without wasting it (< 70% would mean over-provisioning) and without being in danger of throttling (> 90% indicates under-provisioning). No action is needed. Provisioned Throughput doesn't auto-scale.

question_text: A RAG application sends 10 retrieved chunks (each 500 tokens) as context to Bedrock on every request. Analysis shows that on average only 3 chunks are actually relevant to the query. What optimisation reduces cost while maintaining answer quality?

options.text: Always send all 10 chunks to ensure completeness
Apply a reranker to score and select only the top 3 most relevant chunks before sending to the FM, reducing input tokens by ~70%
Use a shorter embedding model to generate smaller vectors
Switch to a model with a larger context window

explanation: A reranker scores all 10 retrieved chunks for relevance to the specific query and selects the top N (e.g., 3) before passing to the FM. This reduces input tokens by ~70% (7 chunks × 500 tokens = 3,500 fewer tokens per request) while improving answer quality (less noise in context). Always sending all 10 wastes 70% of context tokens. Shorter embedding vectors are about retrieval index size, not prompt token count. A larger context window enables more tokens but doesn't reduce cost.
source_topic: Reranker to reduce RAG context tokens sent to FM
